chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Yazid ibn Ishaq from Harun ibn Hamzah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys palm trees to cut them for their trunks, so the man departs and leaves the palms in their original state, uncut. When the man returns, the palms have borne fruit. He said: 'The fruit belongs to him; he may do with it as he wishes, unless the owner of the palms was the one who watered it and tended to it.'

key_terms.يَقُومُ عَلَيْهِ: he tends to it/cares for it

ai.seo_question: Who owns the fruit from palm trees bought for their trunks if they bear fruit before being cut?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the principle of *ghunm* (benefit) following *ghurm* (liability/cost) in agricultural transactions, specifically addressing the ambiguity of fruit ownership when the primary intent was timber. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes that the buyer retains the fruit unless the seller actively maintained and watered the trees, highlighting the Shia legal emphasis on actual labor and care (*qiyam*) as the determinant for entitlement. This ruling underscores the importance of distinguishing between passive ownership and active stewardship in Islamic commercial jurisprudence.
